name: Okara.ai
tagline: A hosted AI assistant workspace: chat with a model, point it at your documents, get drafts and answers back.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Products in this shape are mostly a nice interface wrapped around somebody else's model, and that interface is exactly the thing coding agents are good at. A single session gets you streaming chat, a document library, retrieval over your own files, and saved prompts, running locally against an API key you own. The gaps are the unglamorous parts: mobile access, sync between machines, file parsers that do not choke on real PDFs, and whatever integrations the hosted version quietly does for you. We also cannot verify the exact feature set or price here, so treat this as a verdict on the category rather than a teardown of the product. If the real thing turns out to lean on proprietary data or a tuned model, move this to a firm no.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you chat with an LLM, upload documents into a searchable index, and reuse saved prompts against them.
requirements: An API key for a hosted model provider, or a local model via Ollama
Node 20 and a machine you do not mind leaving on
Willingness to babysit PDF and DOCX parsing
whatYouLose: Mobile and tablet clients that actually feel finished
Cross device sync and shared team workspaces
Whatever connectors the hosted product ships for Drive, Notion, email and friends
Someone else absorbing model deprecations and API changes
Retrieval quality that has been tuned on real usage rather than your first guess at chunk size
moatNotes: Wrappers live and die on the last ten percent: streaming that never stalls, citations that point at the right page, uploads that do not silently fail.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the DIY version is great until you are on your phone in a taxi, or until the PDF parser eats a scanned contract, or until the model you hardcoded gets retired. Paying converts a maintenance job into a subscription, and for most people the subscription is cheaper than their own attention. The other half of it is trust: teams would rather point at a vendor with a security page than at a Docker container on someone's laptop.
notes: Judge this one on your own documents, not on the demo; retrieval quality is where these products separate.
prompt:
Build a local AI assistant workspace. Single user, runs on my machine, no accounts, no telemetry, no cloud database.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js 14 App Router with TypeScript and Tailwind
- SQLite via better-sqlite3 for chats, messages, documents and chunks
- sqlite-vec (or a plain cosine similarity scan if that fails to install) for vector search
- OpenAI-compatible chat and embedding endpoints, base URL and key from .env

In scope:
1. Chat view with streaming responses, markdown rendering, code blocks, and a model picker read from an env list.
2. Conversation list in a sidebar: rename, delete, search by title.
3. Document library: upload PDF, DOCX, TXT and MD. Extract text, chunk at roughly 800 tokens with overlap, embed, store in SQLite.
4. Retrieval: when a chat has documents attached, embed the question, pull the top 8 chunks, inject them into the system prompt, and render citations under the answer that link back to the source chunk text.
5. Saved prompts: name, body, optional variables filled in by a small form before sending.
6. Export any conversation to markdown.

Out of scope: auth, multi user, billing, mobile app, image generation, plugins, web browsing.

Rules:
- All secrets in .env, ship .env.example, never hardcode keys.
- Everything must work offline except the model calls themselves.
- Data lives in ./data/app.db, one command to reset it.
- Handle upload and parse failures visibly instead of swallowing them.
- README with setup, env vars, and a short note on which parsers are flaky.
- Seed script that loads two sample text files so retrieval can be tested immediately.
